terms.def: The first official step for a City Council bill: a member files it, it gets an Intro number, and the Speaker refers it to a committee to study it.
Status for a bill that is sitting with one or more Council committees. While there, members can hold hearings, ask for an analysis of its cost, amend it, and decide whether to vote on it.
Means a Council committee has held a public hearing on the bill, where residents, city agencies, advocates and experts could give testimony for or against it.
The committee took up the bill (often at a hearing) but chose not to vote yet. The bill remains pending in that committee and can come back at a later meeting.
The committee approved the bill by majority vote and sent it on to the full Council for a final vote at a Stated meeting.
The Council's list of items cleared by committee and waiting for a vote of the full Council. A bill placed here needs no further committee action.
The full City Council voted to pass the item. A bill for a local law then goes to the Mayor; a resolution takes effect on the Council's vote alone.
Status used mostly for land use matters (such as rezonings reviewed under ULURP): the Council voted in favor of the resolution approving the application.
The Council has passed the local law and it is awaiting the Mayor. Under the City Charter the Mayor has 30 days to sign it, veto it, or take no action, in which case it becomes law anyway.
The bill is now a local law of New York City, either because the Mayor signed it or because the Mayor's 30 days ran out without a signature or veto.
The Mayor let the 30-day window pass without signing or vetoing the Council-passed bill, so it became law automatically without a signature.
The Mayor formally rejected a bill the Council passed. The Council can still make it law by overriding the veto with a two-thirds vote of its members.
The bill is no longer active. This happens when a committee recommends it be filed (dropped) or when its sponsor leaves the Council.
The Council's four-year legislative session ended before the bill passed, so it expired. To move forward it has to be introduced again in the new session as a new bill.
The bill's sponsor took it out of consideration, so it will not move forward.
The bill came to a vote and failed because more members voted against it than for it.
Status used for land use applications and nominations that the Council voted to reject.
Action on the item has been put off to a later date. This is often seen with land use items that still need negotiation before a vote.
The item is tied to a related bill or resolution in a package and cannot advance until that companion item is passed first.
